scenario: Checkout latency is spiking and some Pods show `Evicted`. Find the sick node, isolate it safely **without breaking PDBs**, and clean up.

steps.output: node/ip-10-0-3-17.eu-central-1.compute.internal cordoned

Fix the requests, add LimitRanges, and let Karpenter replace the node.

title: Incident: Argo CD won't let you roll back
scenario: Argo CD app `payments` auto-synced a bad commit (`9f3c2e1`) and is Degraded. Roll back **now**, then make Git the source of truth again and restore automation.

explore.output:
9f3c2e1 (HEAD -> main, origin/main) payments: bump to 3.1.0
a77d0b4 payments: tune HPA
# automated sync disabled for payments (exploration — no attempt used)

steps.task: Show the app's current health and sync status.
steps.output:
Name:               argocd/payments
Sync Policy:        Automated (Prune)
Sync Status:        Synced to main (9f3c2e1)
Health Status:      Degraded

steps.task: List the app's deployment history to find the last good ID.
Roll back to history ID **11**. (Argo CD has a rule about automated apps…)
steps.blocked: FATA[0000] rpc error: code = FailedPrecondition desc = rollback cannot be initiated when auto-sync is enabled
steps.solution: argocd app set payments --sync-policy none, then: argocd app rollback payments 11
steps.hint: Rollback is refused while automated sync is on. Set the sync policy to `none` first (that command is free), then roll back.
steps.output:
TIMESTAMP                  GROUP  KIND        NAMESPACE  NAME      STATUS  HEALTH
2026-11-16T10:21:04+04:00  apps   Deployment  payments   payments  Synced  Healthy

steps.task: Fix Git: create a commit that reverts `9f3c2e1` on main.

wrong.output: # rewriting shared main history breaks everyone's clones and the audit trail — revert instead

steps.output:
[main 5be81aa] Revert "payments: bump to 3.1.0"
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

steps.task: Push it, then re-enable automated sync for `payments` (one line, `&&` is fine).
steps.solution: git push && argocd app set payments --sync-policy automated --auto-prune --self-heal
steps.output:
To github.com:acme/gitops.git
   9f3c2e1..5be81aa  main -> main

explanation: Argo CD refuses `rollback` on automated apps, because the next sync would undo it. Disable automation, roll back for fast relief, revert in Git so desired state equals the running state, then re-enable sync.

title: Incident: Pods lost the database
scenario: After a Karpenter EC2NodeClass change this morning, `orders` Pods time out connecting to Aurora (`orders-db.cluster-c9x.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com:5432`). New nodes use security group **sg-0nodes789**. The DB uses **sg-0db123**.

explore.output:
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
orders-6f7d8c9b5-k2x8p    0/1     Running   3          14m

steps.task: From inside the `orders` Deployment, test TCP 5432 to the DB endpoint.
steps.output: nc: connect to orders-db.cluster-c9x.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com port 5432 (tcp) failed: Connection timed out

steps.task: Inspect the DB security group `sg-0db123`.
Allow TCP 5432 into `sg-0db123` **from the node security group** `sg-0nodes789` (no CIDRs).
steps.solution: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0db123 --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group sg-0nodes789

wrong.output: # opening a card-data database to the internet = instant PCI finding (and GuardDuty alert)
# node IPs change all the time — reference the security group, not CIDRs

steps.output: { "Return": true, "SecurityGroupRules": [{ "SecurityGroupRuleId": "sgr-0a1b2c3d", "GroupId": "sg-0db123", "IpProtocol": "tcp", "FromPort": 5432, "ToPort": 5432, "ReferencedGroupInfo": { "GroupId": "sg-0nodes789" } }] }

steps.output: Connection to orders-db.cluster-c9x.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com (10.0.21.8) 5432 port [tcp/postgresql] succeeded!

explanation: Group-to-group references survive node churn, and CIDRs don't. The real fix belongs in IaC: add the rule in Terraform (or make the EC2NodeClass `securityGroupSelectorTerms` include the SG the DB trusts), so the console hotfix doesn't drift. Your first test re-runs freely, because earlier commands replay at no cost.

title: Incident: the OOM killer took out nginx
scenario: The payment gateway host's nginx was killed overnight. A batch service `report-worker` runs on the same box. Find out what happened and cap the noisy neighbour **without editing unit files**.

steps.task: Search the kernel log for OOM-killer activity.
steps.hint: The kernel ring buffer (`dmesg -T` or `journalctl -k`), grepped for `oom`.
steps.output:
Nov 16 02:13:44 pay-gw-01 kernel: report-worker invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x140cca, order=0, oom_score_adj=0
Nov 16 02:13:44 pay-gw-01 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 1193 (nginx) total-vm:812344kB, anon-rss:61220kB, oom_score_adj=0
Nov 16 02:13:44 pay-gw-01 kernel: oom_reaper: reaped process 1193 (nginx)

steps.task: Show the top processes by memory right now.
steps.output:
USER   PID   %CPU %MEM    VSZ     RSS   COMMAND
batch  2290  88.1 71.4 9812332 5833112 /usr/bin/python3 /opt/report/worker.py
www    3311   0.4  0.8  81234   61220 nginx: worker process

steps.task: Cap `report-worker.service` at **2G** of memory at runtime (persisted drop-in, no manual unit edits).
steps.hint: `systemctl set-property <unit> MemoryMax=...` writes a drop-in and applies it to the live cgroup.

wrong.output: # MemoryLimit= is the deprecated cgroup-v1 name — use MemoryMax= on cgroup v2

steps.task: Verify the limit is active.
steps.output: MemoryMax=2147483648

explanation: The batch job triggered the OOM, but the kernel picked nginx. cgroup v2 `MemoryMax` makes the worker OOM inside its own cgroup instead, and `MemoryHigh` throttles it before that. Better still: give critical daemons `OOMScoreAdjust=-500`, or isolate batch work on separate nodes.

title: Incident: a secret got merged to main
scenario: PR #482 (merge commit `c0ffee1`) added `config/prod.env` with a live Stripe key, and it's on `main`. Undo the merge safely on a shared branch, then decide what else is required.

explore.output:
commit c0ffee1 (Merge: 8a1d2e0 41bc9f7)
    Merge pull request #482 from acme/feat/billing
 config/prod.env          |  3 +++
 src/billing/client.ts    | 41 +++++++++++++++++++++++++

steps.task: Show the last 3 merge commits on main in one-line form.
steps.output:
c0ffee1 Merge pull request #482 from acme/feat/billing
7d2a9b3 Merge pull request #479 from acme/fix/retries
1e4f0aa Merge pull request #475 from acme/chore/deps

steps.task: Revert merge commit `c0ffee1`, keeping main's side (the first parent).
steps.hint: Merge commits have two parents — tell revert which one is the mainline.

wrong.output:
error: commit c0ffee1 is a merge but no -m option was given.
fatal: revert failed

steps.output:
[main 3fa91c2] Revert "Merge pull request #482 from acme/feat/billing"
 2 files changed, 44 deletions(-)

steps.task: The file is gone from main. What else is **mandatory**? Type `answer A`, `answer B` or `answer C` — A) nothing, the revert removed it · B) rotate/revoke the Stripe key now; it's still in Git history and any clone/fork · C) delete and recreate the repository
steps.output: Correct — revoke in Stripe, review its usage logs, then (optionally) purge history with git filter-repo + force-push and ask GitHub to purge cached views.

explanation: `git revert -m 1` undoes a merge without rewriting shared history. A revert does **not** un-leak a credential, though — the value lives on in history, forks and CI caches. Revoking it is the only real fix. Prevent repeats with push protection, a gitleaks pre-commit hook, and secrets loaded from a manager at runtime.

title: Incident: TLS cert won't renew
scenario: Synthetic checks warn: `api.acme.io` certificate expires in 2 days. cert-manager should have renewed it 28 days ago. The team migrated from ingress-nginx to the AWS Load Balancer Controller last month.

explore.output:
NAME   CLASS   HOSTS         ADDRESS                                        PORTS     AGE
api    alb     api.acme.io   k8s-shop-api-1a2b3c.eu-central-1.elb.amazonaws.com   80, 443   210d

steps.task: List Certificates in all namespaces and spot the one that isn't Ready.
steps.output:
NAMESPACE  NAME       READY   SECRET     AGE
shop       api-tls    False   api-tls    210d
internal   grafana    True    grafana    90d

steps.task: List ACME challenges in namespace `shop`.
steps.output:
NAME                          STATE     DOMAIN        AGE
api-tls-1-2981837726-0        pending   api.acme.io   28d

steps.task: Describe that challenge to see why it's stuck.
steps.output:
Spec:
  Solver:
    http01:
      Ingress:
        Ingress Class Name:  nginx
Status:
  Presented:  true
  Reason:     Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation: wrong status code '404', expected '200'
  State:      pending

steps.task: Root cause? Type `answer A|B|C` — A) Let's Encrypt rate limit · B) the ClusterIssuer's HTTP-01 solver still uses `ingressClassName: nginx`, but traffic now enters via the `alb` class, so the challenge path is never routed · C) the DNS record for api.acme.io is wrong
steps.output: Correct — update the solver (ingressClassName: alb, or switch to DNS-01 with Route 53), then delete the stuck challenge/order so cert-manager retries.

explanation: The solver created a temporary Ingress with class `nginx`, which nobody serves any more, so Let's Encrypt gets a 404. A DNS-01 solver (Route 53 + IRSA or Pod Identity) avoids depending on ingress routing at all. Alert on `certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds` well before 30 days.

title: NAT Gateway drops under load
scenario: During peak, Pods calling one partner API (single IP) get sporadic `connection reset`/timeouts. CloudWatch shows `ErrorPortAllocation > 0` on the NAT Gateway.
question: What's the most accurate explanation and fix?
options: NAT GW supports ~55,000 simultaneous connections per unique destination (IP+port+protocol) per NAT IP — add secondary EIPs to the NAT GW and use keep-alive/connection pooling
The NAT Gateway is out of bandwidth; upgrade to a larger instance type
Security group connection tracking is full; switch to NACLs
DNS throttling on Route 53 Resolver
explanation: Port exhaustion toward one destination is the classic case. Each NAT IP gives ~55k concurrent connections per destination, and a NAT gateway can have multiple (secondary) IPs. Pool HTTP connections — new TLS connections per request burn ports and CPU.

title: DNS latency with ndots:5
scenario: A service calls `api.stripe.com` thousands of times per second. CoreDNS CPU is high and many lookups take 5s.
question: Which statements are TRUE? (select all)
options: With the default `ndots:5`, `api.stripe.com` (2 dots) is first tried with every search domain (`.ns.svc.cluster.local`, `.svc.cluster.local`, …) → several NXDOMAIN round-trips per lookup
Using a trailing dot (`api.stripe.com.`) or `dnsConfig.options: ndots: 2` avoids the search-path expansion
NodeLocal DNSCache reduces CoreDNS load and conntrack race issues for UDP DNS
Raising CPU limits on the application Pod fixes it
explanation: ndots:5 turns one external lookup into several, and the 5s delays are typical of a conntrack UDP race or dropped packets with A+AAAA queries in parallel. Trailing dots, lower ndots, NodeLocal DNSCache and client-side caching all help. App CPU limits are unrelated.

title: etcd quorum
question: A self-managed control plane runs a **4-member** etcd cluster. How many members can fail while it keeps quorum, and is 4 better than 3?
options: 1 — same tolerance as 3 members, with more write latency; use odd sizes (3 or 5)
2 — quorum is 50%
3 — any one member can serve
0 — even-sized clusters never reach quorum
explanation: Quorum = ⌊n/2⌋+1. For n=4 that's 3, so you tolerate 1 failure — exactly like n=3, but with an extra vote to wait for on every write. 5 members tolerate 2.

title: Karpenter keeps killing my batch jobs
scenario: Long-running (2h) report Jobs get interrupted when Karpenter consolidates under-utilised nodes.
question: Which are valid ways to protect them? (select all)
options: Annotate the Pods with `karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true"`
Use a dedicated NodePool for batch with `consolidationPolicy: WhenEmpty` and/or disruption `budgets`
Make the Jobs checkpoint and be idempotent so interruptions (including Spot reclaims) are survivable
Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0` so Pods stop faster
explanation: do-not-disrupt blocks voluntary disruption of nodes running those Pods. A separate pool with gentler consolidation and budgets limits churn, and checkpointing covers involuntary events such as Spot interruptions. A zero grace period only makes things worse.

title: Karpenter v1 NodePool
scenario: Allow Spot **and** On-Demand capacity and consolidate empty or under-utilised nodes after 1 minute, using the `default` EC2NodeClass.
template:
apiVersion: {{api}}
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: general
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: {{nck}}
        name: default
      requirements:
        - key: {{key}}
          operator: In
          values: ["spot", "on-demand"]
        - key: kubernetes.io/arch
          operator: In
          values: ["amd64", "arm64"]
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: {{policy}}
    consolidateAfter: 1m
  limits:
    cpu: "200"
explanation: Karpenter v1 (`karpenter.sh/v1`) uses `nodeClassRef` with group, kind and name. The capacity-type key selects Spot or On-Demand (Karpenter favours Spot when both are allowed), and `WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized` replaced v1beta1's `WhenUnderutilized`. Mixing arm64 and amd64 needs multi-arch images.

title: IRSA: AccessDenied on AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
scenario: Pod `api` uses ServiceAccount `api` in namespace **payments**. Its AWS SDK fails with `Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`. Which line is wrong?
explanation: The `sub` must be exactly `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa>`, and the namespace is `payments`, not `payment`. EKS Pod Identity avoids hand-written trust conditions entirely: its trust principal is `pods.eks.amazonaws.com`, with associations managed by the EKS API.

title: Postgres major upgrade with minimal downtime
question: Order the steps for a PostgreSQL 15 → 17 upgrade on RDS using Blue/Green Deployments.
items: Check extension/parameter-group compatibility and take a manual snapshot
Create a Blue/Green deployment with the green environment on PostgreSQL 17 (new parameter group)
Wait for replication to catch up; run read-only validation and performance tests against green
Switch over (writes pause briefly; endpoints are renamed to green)
Monitor, keep blue for a rollback window, then delete the old blue environment
explanation: Blue/Green keeps green in sync through logical replication. The switchover renames endpoints, so apps keep their DNS names, and it typically takes under a minute. Test against green before switching, and keep blue until you're confident.

title: Supply-chain gate for prod
scenario: Design an admission gate so only artifacts built by your pipeline can run in the `prod` cluster.
question: Which controls together achieve that? (select all)
options: Sign images keylessly with cosign in CI (OIDC identity of the workflow)
Admission policy (Kyverno verifyImages / Sigstore policy-controller) that verifies the signature **and** the expected signer identity/issuer
Require images by digest and attach SLSA provenance/SBOM attestations, verified at admission
Allow `:latest` tags so rollouts pick up fixes automatically
explanation: A signature alone isn't enough — you also verify *who* signed (e.g. `https://github.com/acme/app/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main`). Digests bind the policy to the exact bytes, and attestations prove how the image was built. Mutable tags defeat all of it.

title: Self-hosted AI SRE agent on EKS
scenario: You deploy an LLM-powered SRE agent in the cluster. It reads Prometheus/Loki and can run read-only kubectl to investigate payment failures.
question: Which design choices are sound? (select all)
options: Bind its ServiceAccount to a read-only ClusterRole that excludes `secrets` (no `get/list secrets`)
Treat log lines and alert annotations as untrusted input — never let them expand the agent's tool permissions
Log every tool call (command, args, result size) for audit, and require human approval for any mutating action
Give it cluster-admin so investigations are never blocked
explanation: Logs can contain attacker-controlled strings (prompt injection through user agents, headers or error messages). Least-privilege RBAC without Secrets, a full audit trail, and human-in-the-loop for writes keep an AI agent from becoming a new privileged attack path.

title: Incident: refactor wants to destroy the audit bucket
scenario: A teammate moved `aws_s3_bucket.logs` into a new `module "logging"` (resource `aws_s3_bucket.this`). The PR's plan wants to destroy and recreate the bucket holding 3 years of PCI audit logs. Fix the state so the plan is clean — **without** destroying anything.

steps.task: Run the plan and read it carefully.
List the addresses currently in state.
steps.output:
aws_iam_role.app
aws_s3_bucket.logs
aws_s3_bucket_versioning.logs

steps.task: Move the bucket's state entry to its new address (CLI).

wrong.output: # that would DESTROY the audit bucket (and fail anyway: BucketNotEmpty) — never apply a plan with an unexpected destroy
Error: Resource already managed by Terraform — aws_s3_bucket.logs still owns it in state

steps.output:
Move "aws_s3_bucket.logs" to "module.logging.aws_s3_bucket.this"
Successfully moved 1 object(s).

steps.task: The versioning resource moved too (`module.logging.aws_s3_bucket_versioning.this`). Move it as well.
steps.output:
Move "aws_s3_bucket_versioning.logs" to "module.logging.aws_s3_bucket_versioning.this"
Successfully moved 1 object(s).

steps.task: Prove the plan is clean.
steps.output: No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

steps.task: For staging and dev, which approach is better? Type `answer A|B|C` — A) run the same `state mv` by hand in each environment · B) commit `moved { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs  to = module.logging.aws_s3_bucket.this }` blocks so every workspace migrates on its next plan/apply, reviewed in the PR · C) `terraform taint` the bucket
steps.output: Correct — moved blocks are declarative, reviewable and idempotent. Also add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to the audit bucket.

explanation: When you refactor addresses, Terraform sees a delete plus an add. `state mv` fixes one state by hand, while `moved` blocks (Terraform ≥1.1) fix every state through code review. On critical data stores, `prevent_destroy` turns this whole class of mistake into a plan error.

title: Incident: deploy.sh wiped /opt on staging
scenario: Last night's CI deploy ran `deploy.sh` on staging and every directory under `/opt` vanished, not just the app's. The script "worked fine for months". Find out why and pick the guardrail.

steps.task: Lint the script with ShellCheck.
steps.output:
In deploy.sh line 3:
TARGET=$BASE_DIR/$APP
       ^-------^ SC2154 (warning): BASE_DIR is referenced but not assigned.

In deploy.sh line 4:
cd $TARGET/..
^-----------^ SC2164 (warning): Use 'cd ... || exit' in case cd fails.

In deploy.sh line 5:
rm -rf $TARGET/*
       ^------^ SC2115 (warning): Use "${var:?}" to ensure this never expands to /* .

steps.task: Trace a run with `BASE_DIR` unset (as in CI) to see what `rm` really received. (The trace is safe here — this lab's shell is a sandbox.)
steps.hint: `bash -x script args` prints every command after expansion.
steps.output:
+ APP=opt
+ TARGET=/opt
+ cd /opt/..
+ rm -rf /opt/adot /opt/aws /opt/payments /opt/containerd /opt/jumpserver

steps.task: Root cause? Type `answer A|B|C` — A) `BASE_DIR` was never exported in the new CI job, so `$BASE_DIR/$APP` collapsed to `/$APP`, and the job passed `opt` · B) a ShellCheck bug · C) `rm` is aliased to `rm -rf /`
steps.output: Correct — an unset variable silently expanded to an empty string.

steps.task: Which one line at the top makes the script **fail fast** on unset variables and errors? Type `answer A|B|C` — A) `set -euo pipefail` · B) `set -x` · C) `ulimit -n 4096`
steps.output: Correct — with set -u, line 3 dies with 'BASE_DIR: unbound variable' before rm runs. Also use "${TARGET:?}" and quote every expansion.

explanation: Unquoted, unset variables plus `rm -rf` is how a script 'that worked for months' deletes a server. Use `set -euo pipefail`, `${VAR:?}` on anything destructive, `cd ... || exit`, quote every expansion, and run ShellCheck in CI — it flagged all three bugs before anything ran.
